theory.intro: Reading the inverse trig derivatives backwards gives two standard integrals, with $a>0$. The shape $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}$ integrates to $\arcsin\dfrac{x}{a}$, and $\dfrac{1}{a^{2}+x^{2}}$ integrates to $\dfrac{1}{a}\arctan\dfrac{x}{a}$. Only the second carries a factor $\dfrac{1}{a}$.
facts: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}=\arcsin\dfrac{x}{a}+C$, with no extra factor in front.
$\displaystyle\int\dfrac{-dx}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}=\arccos\dfrac{x}{a}+C$: the same shape with the sign reversed.
Read $a$ as the square root of the constant, so $9+x^{2}$ has $a=3$.

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}$ exists only for $|x|<a$. A definite integral can still have an endpoint at $x=-a$ or $x=a$: these improper integrals converge, and endpoint values of the primitive are evaluated through limits from inside the interval.
Take any constant factor outside the integral before matching the shape.
When $x$ carries a coefficient, factor it out first, as in $\sqrt{16-9x^{2}}=3\sqrt{\dfrac{16}{9}-x^{2}}$.
Reversing the chain rule gives $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{1+[f(x)]^{2}}\,dx=\arctan f(x)+C$.
Every indefinite integral needs $+C$, and a definite integral does not.
Check any primitive by differentiating it back.
steps: Match the integrand to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}$ or $\dfrac{1}{a^{2}+x^{2}}$, and read off $a$.
Take any constant factor outside the integral.

For a definite integral, substitute the upper limit and subtract the value at the lower limit. At an endpoint where the integrand is undefined, evaluate the primitive through a limit from inside the interval.

workedExamples.solution_text:
Factor out the constant and identify $a=8$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{4}{\sqrt{64-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=4\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{64-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=4\arcsin\frac{x}{8}+C\end{aligned}$

Here $a=7$. The arctangent primitive requires the factor $\frac{1}{7}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{15}{49+x^{2}}\,dx\\&=15\int\frac{1}{49+x^{2}}\,dx\\&=\frac{15}{7}\arctan\frac{x}{7}+C\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Find $\int\frac{-3}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}\,dx$, expressing the answer using inverse cosine.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The negative numerator matches the inverse cosine derivative.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{-3}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=3\int\frac{-1}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=3\arccos\frac{x}{4}+C\end{aligned}$

Factor out the coefficient of $x^{2}$ before matching the standard form.
$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{25-16x^{2}}&=4\sqrt{\frac{25}{16}-x^{2}}\end{aligned}$
Here $a=\frac{5}{4}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{2}{\sqrt{25-16x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{25}{16}-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=\frac{1}{2}\arcsin\frac{4x}{5}+C\end{aligned}$

(a) The integrand is undefined at $x=4$. Evaluate the convergent improper integral through a limit from below.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{16-x^{2}}}\,dx\\&=\lim_{b\to4^{-}}\left[\arcsin\frac{x}{4}\right]_{0}^{b}\\&=\frac{\pi}{2}-0\\&=\frac{\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$
(b)
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{0}^{4\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{16+x^{2}}\,dx\\&=\left[\frac{1}{4}\arctan\frac{x}{4}\right]_{0}^{4\sqrt{3}}\\&=\frac{1}{4}\arctan\sqrt{3}-\frac{1}{4}\arctan0\\&=\frac{\pi}{12}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: A curve has $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{5}{25+x^{2}}$ and passes through $(5,\frac{\pi}{2})$. Find its equation.

workedExamples.solution_text:
Write $1-9x^{6}=1-(3x^{3})^{2}$. For $f(x)=3x^{3}$, the required numerator is $f'(x)=9x^{2}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\frac{5x^{2}}{\sqrt{1-9x^{6}}}\,dx\\&=\frac{5}{9}\int\frac{9x^{2}}{\sqrt{1-(3x^{3})^{2}}}\,dx\\&=\frac{5}{9}\arcsin(3x^{3})+C\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: Find the exact area bounded by $y=\frac{8}{16+x^{2}}$, the $x$-axis, and the lines $x=-4$ and $x=4\sqrt{3}$.

foundation.question_text: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}\,dx$, giving the answer as an inverse cosine.
foundation.solution_text:
Here $a=3$, and the integrand is the derivative of $\arccos\dfrac{x}{3}$.
$\displaystyle\int\dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}\,dx=\arccos\dfrac{x}{3}+C$

Here $a=1$, so the factor $\dfrac{1}{a}$ is $1$.
$\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{1+x^{2}}=\arctan x+C$

development.question_text: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{-5}{\sqrt{1-4x^{2}}}\,dx$, giving the answer as an inverse cosine.

A curve has $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4-x^{2}}}$ and passes through $(0,\pi)$.
Find its equation.

A curve has $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3}{9+x^{2}}$ and $y=\pi$ when $x=3$.
Find its equation.

mastery.solution_text:
The curve is above the $x$-axis throughout, so the area is the integral.
$\text{Area}=\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2\sqrt{3}}\dfrac{6}{4+x^{2}}\,dx$
$=\left[6\times\dfrac{1}{2}\arctan\dfrac{x}{2}\right]_{-2}^{2\sqrt{3}}$
$=3\arctan\sqrt{3}-3\arctan(-1)$
$=3\times\dfrac{\pi}{3}+3\times\dfrac{\pi}{4}$
$=\pi+\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$
$=\dfrac{7\pi}{4}$ square units
